title: Industrial zones
legendIntro: Colour shows which of Carlota Perez's five technological revolutions the zone's main product belonged to in the period shown.
note: Outlines are approximate. Some follow today's district borders, and others are drawn by hand from named landmarks, so use them as a guide, not a survey. Zones were chosen from company and city histories; the revolution for each period is a judgement about what the main plant made.
source: Zone records and revolution assignments compiled from company and city histories, with fact checks applied to the text.

categories.name: First: mechanised textiles, water power (from 1771)
categories.short: First revolution: mechanised textiles, water power

categories.name: Second: steam, iron and railways (from 1829)
categories.short: Second revolution: steam, iron and railways

categories.name: Third: steel, electricity, heavy engineering (from 1875)
categories.short: Third revolution: steel, electricity, heavy engineering

categories.name: Fourth: oil, cars, mass production (from 1908)
categories.short: Fourth revolution: oil, cars, mass production

1880s.name: Koishikawa army arsenal
lines: Rifles and ammunition were made from iron on steam-driven machine tools.
1880s.note: The army's main arsenal sat in the old Mito domain garden. It was Tokyo's largest factory.

1909.name: Koishikawa army arsenal
lines: The war-expanded arsenal made steel rifles and ammunition with smokeless powder.
1909.note: Wars with China and Russia expanded the arsenal. It was still the largest factory in the city.

1930s.name: Koishikawa army arsenal (moved)
lines: The arsenal had moved to Kokura and Kōrakuen stadium stood on the site.
Last industrial use: third revolution (steel, electricity, heavy engineering)
1930s.note: The arsenal moved to Kokura after the 1923 earthquake, finishing in 1935. Kōrakuen baseball stadium opened on the site in 1937.

1880s.name: Itabashi gunpowder works
lines: Black powder was milled by water wheels on the Shakujii River.
1880s.note: The army's first modern powder works, opened in 1876 on a Kaga domain estate. Water wheels on the Shakujii River drove it.

1909.name: Itabashi gunpowder works
lines: The works made modern explosives, a heavy-chemicals product.
1909.note: The powder works grew to about 50 hectares with hundreds of buildings.

1880s.name: Ōji and the northern works
lines: Machine papermaking at Ōji paper was the defining plant; the printing works stood beside it.
1880s.note: Shibusawa Eiichi's paper company opened at Ōji in 1875. The government printing works stood beside it.

1909.name: Ōji and the northern works
lines: The Ōji paper mill was still the zone's defining plant; the new Jūjō arsenal branch was smaller.
1909.note: An arsenal branch opened at Jūjō in 1905 beside the paper mill. Factories spread along the Shakujii River.

1930s.name: Ōji, Jūjō, Itabashi and Akabane
1930s.ja: 王子・十条・板橋・赤羽
lines: Arsenals, the powder works and the clothing depot made it an army belt of steel arms and explosives.
1930s.note: Arsenals, the powder works and the army clothing depot made this an army workshop belt. Chemical and printing plants filled gaps.

1945.name: Ōji, Jūjō, Itabashi and Akabane
1945.ja: 王子・十条・板橋・赤羽
lines: Wartime arsenals making munitions and gunpowder defined the zone.
1945.note: Wartime arsenals worked at full stretch until the April 1945 raids. Afterward the US army took over several sites.

1960s.name: Ōji, Itabashi and Akabane
lines: Printing, optics and precision instruments for the mass market defined Itabashi.
1960s.note: Former army sites became factories, schools and US bases. Itabashi grew into a printing and optics district.

today.name: Itabashi and Akabane works
lines: The remaining printing and optics firms make mass-market goods.
today.note: Itabashi keeps printing and optics firms, far fewer than before. The powder works is a national historic site.

1880s.name: Senju wool mill and Arakawa
lines: The state mill spun and wove wool cloth by machine.
1880s.note: The state wool mill opened in 1879 to make uniform cloth at home. It began Japan's wool industry.

1909.name: Senju wool mill and Arakawa
lines: The expanded wool mill was still the defining plant; leather and chemical works were small.
1909.note: The wool mill expanded for the Russo-Japanese War. Small leather and chemical works gathered nearby.

1930s.name: Senju and Arakawa works
lines: The wool mill still made uniform cloth and defined the zone, among small leather, chemical and metal shops.
1930s.note: Small factories packed Mikawashima, Machiya and Ogu inside the Sumida loop. The wool mill still made uniform cloth.
1930s.made: wool cloth, leather, chemicals, small metal

1945.name: Senju and Arakawa works
lines: The wool mill made uniform cloth to the end; munitions parts came from small shops.
1945.note: The wool mill made uniform cloth to the end. Air raids burned much of Arakawa's small-factory district.

1960s.name: Senju and Arakawa works
lines: With the mill closed, small metal, leather and printing workshops made mass-market goods and parts.
1960s.note: Small workshops filled Arakawa. The wool mill closed; Tokyo Stadium opened on its site in 1962.

today.name: Senju (former wool mill)
lines: The mill site is the Arakawa Sports Center.
Last industrial use: first revolution (mechanised textiles, water power)
today.note: The Arakawa Sports Center (1984) stands on the mill site. A stretch of the 1911–14 brick wall survives.

1880s.name: Fukagawa and Ōjima
lines: Cement and bricks were fired in coal kilns and shipped by canal.
1880s.note: The state cement works at Fukagawa, sold to Asano in 1884, used canal transport. Most of the east bank was still town and fields.

1909.name: Fukagawa and Ōjima
lines: Chemical fertiliser and machinery joined cement, making heavy chemicals the defining industry.
1909.note: Canals drew cement, fertilizer and machine works. Spinning and reeling mills came too.

1930s.name: Fukagawa, Ōjima and Sunamachi
lines: Steel, cement, chemicals and machinery plants filled the former farmland.
1930s.note: Heavy plants took cheap former farmland east of the Yokojikken canal. The new Arakawa floodway (1930) marked the east edge.

1945.name: Fukagawa, Ōjima and Sunamachi
lines: Surviving steel and chemical plants defined the zone.
1945.note: Burned in the March 1945 raid. Some large plants survived and restarted after 1946.

1960s.name: Fukagawa, Ōjima and Sunamachi
lines: Steel, chemicals and machinery plants remained, though shrinking.
1960s.note: Pollution rules and land prices pushed large plants out. Ōjima's big sites became public housing estates.

today.name: Ōjima and Sunamachi (former plants)
lines: Former plant sites are housing estates, schools and shops.
Last industrial use: third revolution (steel, electricity, heavy engineering)
today.note: Former plant sites are housing estates, schools and shopping centres.

features.name: Ishikawajima (former shipyard)
features.ja: 石川島跡（大川端リバーシティ21）

1880s.name: Ishikawajima shipyard
lines: The yard built iron steamships and marine steam engines.
1880s.note: A private shipyard on the island at the Sumida mouth. It grew out of a domain yard of the 1850s.

1909.name: Ishikawajima shipyard
lines: Steel steamships and boilers for the navy defined the yard.
1909.note: The yard built steamships and boilers for the navy and coastal lines.

1930s.name: Ishikawajima shipyard
lines: Steel shipbuilding stayed the core; aircraft engines were a side line.
1930s.note: The yard also made cars and aircraft for a time. It opened a second yard at Toyosu in 1939.

1945.name: Ishikawajima shipyard
lines: Steel warships and landing craft.
1945.note: Both Ishikawajima yards built for the navy. Repair work restarted under occupation.

1960s.name: Ishikawajima shipyard
lines: Steel ships and heavy machinery.
1960s.note: Now Ishikawajima-Harima Heavy Industries. The old island yard was cramped beside the new Toyosu site.

today.name: Ishikawajima (former shipyard)
today.ja: 石川島跡（大川端リバーシティ21）
lines: Ōkawabata River City 21 towers stand on the yard.
Last industrial use: third revolution (steel, electricity, heavy engineering)
today.note: The yard closed in 1979. Ōkawabata River City 21 towers stand on it.

1880s.name: Shibaura and Shinagawa shore
lines: Tanaka's works made telegraph equipment, a second-revolution technology in Perez.
1880s.note: Tanaka's machine works, later Toshiba, opened in 1882; a state glass works stood at Shinagawa. Both were small.

1909.name: Shibaura and Shinagawa shore
lines: Shibaura Seisakusho made generators and motors.
1909.note: Shibaura Seisakusho made generators and motors on reclaimed land. Shibaura's fill began about 1906.

1930s.name: Shibaura and Shinagawa shore
lines: Heavy electrical machinery defined reclaimed Shibaura.
1930s.note: Reclaimed Shibaura held electrical works and a growing harbour. Shibaura Seisakusho merged into Toshiba in 1939.

1945.name: Shibaura and Shinagawa shore
lines: Electrical machinery works.
1945.note: Bombed in 1945. The occupation army then used the Shibaura piers.

1960s.name: Shibaura and Shinagawa shore
lines: Port warehouses and trucking replaced the factories as the main use.
1960s.note: Factories gave way to port warehouses and trucking. Toshiba moved production to the suburbs.

1880s.name: Kawaguchi foundries
lines: Coke-fired foundries cast iron pots and kettles.
1880s.note: An old casting town across the Arakawa, using local sand and clay. It made household pots and kettles.

1909.name: Kawaguchi foundries
lines: Foundries still cast iron household goods.
1909.note: Foundries multiplied, still mostly making household goods.

1930s.name: Kawaguchi foundries
lines: Castings for machines and the army fed heavy engineering.
1930s.note: Foundries turned to castings for machines and the army.

1945.name: Kawaguchi foundries
lines: Munitions castings.
1945.note: Foundries cast for the army until the end.

1960s.name: Kawaguchi foundries
lines: Machine castings fed the car and machinery boom.
1960s.note: Several hundred foundries worked here in the boom years.

today.name: Kawaguchi (former foundries)
lines: Few foundries remain; tower blocks replaced them.
Last industrial use: fourth revolution (oil, cars, mass production)
today.note: After the 1970s oil shocks foundries closed or moved. Tower blocks for Tokyo commuters replaced them.

1909.name: Kanegafuchi and Mukōjima mills
lines: Kanegafuchi and its neighbours were mechanised cotton-spinning and muslin mills.
1909.note: Kanegafuchi Spinning opened in 1889 at the Sumida bend. Cotton and muslin mills followed along the river.

1930s.name: Kanegafuchi and Mukōjima mills
lines: Cotton and muslin mills lined the east bank.
1930s.note: Kanegafuchi, Fuji Gas Spinning and Tokyo Muslin mills lined the east bank. Thousands of young women worked the spindles.

1945.name: Kanegafuchi and Mukōjima mills
lines: Spindles were scrapped and the mills turned to metal munitions.
1945.note: Spindles were scrapped for metal and mills turned to war work. The March 1945 fire raid burned the east bank.

1960s.name: Kanegafuchi and Mukōjima mills
lines: The shrinking Kanebō cotton mill still defined the zone until 1969.
1960s.note: The big mills shrank and left. Kanebō's founding Tokyo mill closed in 1969.

today.name: Kanegafuchi (former Kanebō mill)
lines: The mill site holds flats and a park.
Last industrial use: first revolution (mechanised textiles, water power)
today.note: Shirahige-higashi apartment blocks and Kanebō park stand on the mill site. A stone marks the company's birthplace.

1909.name: Honjō and Kameido works
lines: Seikōsha clocks, soap, rubber and machinery were light metal and chemical goods of the steel and electricity age.
1909.note: Light industry arrived after the 1894–95 war. Seikōsha opened its clock factory here in 1892.

1930s.name: Honjō and Kameido works
lines: Small workshops made soap, rubber, glass and machinery, before mass production reached them.
1930s.note: Rebuilt after the 1923 fire, packed with small workshops and workers' housing. Tokyo Muslin's Kameido mill stood here.

1945.name: Honjō and Kameido works
lines: Small workshops did war production in metal and chemicals.
1945.note: The 10 March 1945 raid burned almost all of Honjō. The air photos show bare ground.

1960s.name: Honjō and Kameido works
lines: Family workshops made metal parts, rubber, knitwear and toys for the mass-consumption boom.
1960s.note: Thousands of family workshops rebuilt the district. Sumida ward counted 9,703 factories at its 1970 peak.
1960s.made: metal parts, rubber, knitwear, toys, leather

today.name: Sumida small workshops
lines: The remaining workshops make metal parts, knitwear and prototypes for mass-produced goods.
today.note: Fewer than half the 1970 workshops remain, scattered among flats. The ward promotes them as craft and prototype makers.

1909.name: Ōsaki and the Meguro River
lines: Machinery and metal parts for the steel and electricity age.
1909.note: Factories came to Ōsaki station and the Meguro River late in Meiji. Subcontracting workshops spread around them.

1930s.name: Ōsaki and the Meguro River
lines: Meidensha heavy electrical machinery defined the riverside; camera makers were smaller.
1930s.note: Meidensha, camera and instrument makers lined the Meguro River. Workers' housing mixed with workshops.

1945.name: Ōsaki and the Meguro River
lines: Precision machinery for the war effort.
1945.note: Bombed in the May 1945 raids. Small shops restarted quickly; Sony began in a Gotenyama hut in 1947.

1960s.name: Ōsaki and the Meguro River
lines: Sony's transistor radios and televisions were mass-produced consumer electronics.
1960s.note: Sony grew from Gotenyama to a global firm. Meidensha and small shops still lined the river.

today.name: Ōsaki (former factory belt)
lines: The riverside factories became office towers.
Last industrial use: fourth revolution (oil, cars, mass production)
today.note: Redevelopment from the 1980s turned the riverside factories into office towers.

1909.name: Kawasaki works
lines: Tokyo Electric's light-bulb works defined the first plants; Meiji sugar and machinery came too.
1909.note: The first large plants came to Kawasaki: Meiji sugar in 1906, Tokyo Electric's bulb works in 1908. The shore was still fishing villages.

1930s.name: Kawasaki shore (Asano landfill)
lines: Steel and cement plants took the Asano landfill.
1930s.note: Asano Sōichirō's landfill (1913–28) created new shore at Asano-chō and Shiraishi-chō. Steel and cement plants took it.

1945.name: Kawasaki shore
lines: Steel and munitions.
1945.note: Bombed in April 1945. Steel plants restarted slowly under occupation.

1960s.name: Kawasaki shore
lines: The new landfill's refineries and petrochemicals defined the zone, beside older steel.
1960s.note: New landfill at Chidori-chō and Ukishima added refineries and petrochemicals. Smoke caused the Kawasaki asthma cases.

today.name: Kawasaki shore
lines: Oil refining, chemicals and power remain; steelmaking ended in 2023.
today.note: Ōgishima landfill (1970s) took the steelworks, whose blast furnace stopped in 2023. Refineries, chemicals and power remain.
today.made: oil, chemicals, power, logistics; steel ended 2023

features.name: Minato Mirai (former shipyard)
features.ja: みなとみらい（旧横浜船渠）

1909.name: Yokohama Dock
lines: Stone docks repaired and built steel ships.
1909.note: Yokohama Dock opened its stone docks in the 1890s near Sakuragichō.

1930s.name: Yokohama Dock
lines: Steel merchant ships.
1930s.note: The dock became Mitsubishi's Yokohama shipyard in 1935.

1945.name: Yokohama Dock
1945.ja: 三菱重工業横浜造船所
lines: Steel warships and merchant ships.
1945.note: Mitsubishi's yard built for the navy.

1960s.name: Mitsubishi Yokohama shipyard
1960s.ja: 三菱重工業横浜造船所
lines: Steel shipbuilding at the stone docks.
1960s.note: The shipyard still worked the stone docks by Sakuragichō.

today.name: Minato Mirai (former shipyard)
today.ja: みなとみらい（旧横浜船渠）
lines: Minato Mirai's towers and museums stand on the yard.
Last industrial use: third revolution (steel, electricity, heavy engineering)
today.note: The shipyard left in 1983. Minato Mirai's towers rose on it; one stone dock holds the Nippon Maru.

1909.name: Hachiōji silk weaving
lines: Silk weaving.
1909.note: An old silk-weaving town in the western hills, close to the raw silk of Tama and Kai.

1930s.name: Hachiōji silk weaving
lines: Silk and rayon weaving on power looms; weaving is still mechanised textiles.
1930s.note: Weaving mechanised with power looms. Rayon joined silk.

1930s.name: Toyosu waterfront
lines: Ishikawajima's new yard built steel ships.
1930s.note: Landfill made from harbour dredging was finished in 1937. Ishikawajima's new yard opened here in 1939.

1945.name: Toyosu waterfront
lines: The yard built steel ships for the navy.
1945.note: The Toyosu yard built ships for the navy.

1960s.name: Toyosu waterfront
lines: The steel shipyard defined the landfill; the gas works and power station were secondary.
1960s.note: Shipyard, Tokyo Gas works (1956) and a power station shared the landfill.

today.name: Toyosu (former shipyard and gas works)
lines: Towers, offices and the fish market replaced shipyard and gas works.
Last industrial use: third revolution (steel, electricity, heavy engineering)
today.note: The shipyard closed in April 2001. Tower blocks, offices and the Toyosu market (2018) replaced shipyard and gas works.

1930s.name: Kamata and Ōmori machine shops
lines: Machine shops made parts, tools and electrical goods for heavy industry.
1930s.note: Factories moved out here after the 1923 earthquake. Fields around Kamata filled with machine shops and their subcontractors.

1945.name: Kamata and Ōmori machine shops
lines: Machine shops made weapons parts.
1945.note: The April 1945 raid burned Kamata. Machine shops restarted on pots and repairs.

1960s.name: Kamata and Ōmori machine shops
lines: Small shops made parts and moulds for the car and electronics boom.
1960s.note: Thousands of small shops served the car and electronics boom. New landfill at Heiwajima and Keihinjima added sites.

today.name: Ōta workshops
lines: Precision parts, prototypes and moulds for mass-produced cars and electronics.
today.note: Ōta still has Tokyo's largest cluster of small machine shops, about a third of its 1980s count.

features.name: Tsurumi and Kanagawa shore
features.ja: 京浜・鶴見・神奈川臨海部

1930s.name: Tsurumi and Kanagawa shore
1930s.ja: 京浜・鶴見・神奈川臨海部
lines: Steel and shipyards dominated the new landfill; Nissan's car plant was the newcomer.
1930s.note: New landfill from Namamugi to Moriya-chō drew shipyards and steel. Nissan opened its Yokohama car plant in 1933–35.

1945.name: Tsurumi and Kanagawa shore
1945.ja: 京浜・鶴見・神奈川臨海部
lines: Steel and ships, with trucks secondary.
1945.note: Bombed in 1945; the US army requisitioned parts of the shore. Industry stagnated until the Korean War.

1960s.name: Tsurumi and Kanagawa shore
1960s.ja: 京浜・鶴見・神奈川臨海部
lines: Steel and shipyards still dominated, beside Nissan's engine plant.
1960s.note: Daikoku-chō landfill extended the shore. Nissan's Yokohama plant made engines.

today.name: Tsurumi and Kanagawa shore
today.ja: 京浜・鶴見・神奈川臨海部
lines: Nissan's engine plant, power stations and docks define the shore.
today.note: Nissan's Yokohama engine plant and power stations remain. Daikoku is now mostly docks and warehouses.

1930s.name: Nambu line electrical works
lines: Electrical and telephone-exchange equipment of the electrical age.
1930s.note: Electrical makers such as NEC and Tokyo Electric opened plants among Kawasaki's fields along the new Nambu line.

1945.name: Nambu line electrical works
lines: Radios, radar and communications gear for the forces, still electrical-age technology.
1945.note: Electrical plants made communications equipment for the forces.

1960s.name: Nambu line electrical works
lines: Fujitsu, NEC and Toshiba made computers and electronic telephone equipment.
1960s.note: Fujitsu, NEC and Toshiba plants made this Japan's electronics corridor.

today.name: Musashi-Kosugi (former factories)
lines: Tower blocks replaced the factories; Fujitsu and NEC research sites nearby would be fifth-revolution.
Last industrial use: fifth revolution (information and telecommunications)
today.note: Tower blocks replaced factories around Musashi-Kosugi. Fujitsu and NEC keep research sites nearby.

1930s.name: Nakajima aircraft engine works
1930s.ja: 中島飛行機武蔵製作所
lines: Nakajima made aircraft engines.
1930s.note: Nakajima opened its Musashino engine works in 1938 among farm fields, at the army's request.

1945.name: Nakajima Musashi works
1945.ja: 中島飛行機武蔵製作所
lines: Aircraft engines on a mass scale.
1945.note: About 50,000 people worked here, including students. It was the first target of the B-29 raids, bombed nine times from November 1944.

today.name: Musashino (former Nakajima works)
lines: Park, flats, hospital and city hall.
Last industrial use: fourth revolution (oil, cars, mass production)
today.note: Musashino Central Park, flats, a hospital and the city hall stand on the site.

1930s.name: Tachikawa aircraft works
1930s.ja: 立川飛行機・陸軍航空
lines: Tachikawa Hikōki built army aircraft.
1930s.note: Ishikawajima's aircraft arm moved beside the Tachikawa army airfield in 1930. It became Tachikawa Hikōki in 1936.

1945.name: Tachikawa, Akishima and Higashiyamato plants
1945.ja: 立川・昭島・東大和の航空工場
lines: Army aircraft and engines.
1945.note: Tachikawa Hikōki, the army air arsenal, Shōwa Hikōki and Hitachi's engine plant filled the plateau. Raids in 1945 scattered production.

1960s.name: Tachikawa airfield (US base)
lines: A US air base, not a factory; Shōwa Hikōki's parts works was a remnant.
Last industrial use: fourth revolution (oil, cars, mass production)
1960s.note: The airfield and arsenal were a US air base until 1977. Shōwa Hikōki survived at Akishima making parts.

today.name: Tachikawa (former airfield)
lines: Shōwa Kinen Park and government offices.
Last industrial use: fourth revolution (oil, cars, mass production)
today.note: Returned in 1977, the airfield is now Shōwa Kinen Park and government offices.

1945.name: Hino and Fuchū works
lines: Hino trucks and tanks defined the zone; Toshiba Fuchū made electrical gear.
1945.note: War-era branch plants opened here: Toshiba at Fuchū (1940) and Hino's truck and tank works (1942).

1960s.name: Hino, Fuchū and Murayama works
lines: Hino trucks and Prince cars defined the machinery belt.
1960s.note: Hino trucks, Toshiba Fuchū and Prince's Murayama car plant (1962) made the west a machinery belt.

today.name: Hino and Fuchū works
lines: Hino trucks, though leaving, still define it; Toshiba Fuchū makes heavy electrical gear.
today.note: Nissan's Murayama plant closed in 2004 and Hino is moving out. Toshiba Fuchū still works.

features.name: Kōtō landfill shore
features.ja: 江東臨海部（東雲・辰巳・塩見）

1960s.name: Kōtō landfill shore
1960s.ja: 江東臨海部（東雲・辰巳・塩見）
lines: Timber ponds, steel stockyards and warehouses served the truck-borne construction boom.
1960s.note: New landfill held timber ponds, steel yards and warehouses. Yumenoshima nearby was a rubbish dump.

1960s.name: Chiba steelworks
lines: An integrated steelworks; steel is third-revolution whatever the opening date.
1960s.note: Kawasaki Steel opened Japan's first postwar integrated steelworks here in 1953 on reclaimed shore. A power station followed in 1959.

today.name: Chiba steelworks
lines: JFE still makes steel here.
today.note: JFE Steel still runs the works. Part of the site is now Chiba's harbour park.

1960s.name: Goi and Ichihara petrochemicals
lines: Oil refining and petrochemicals.
1960s.note: Landfill from the early 1960s drew refineries and chemical complexes. Ichihara became one of Japan's biggest factory towns.

today.name: Ichihara and Sodegaura chemicals
lines: Refining, petrochemicals and power.
today.note: Ichihara ranks second in Japan for factory shipments after Toyota city.

1960s.name: Funabashi and Ichikawa shore
lines: Oil storage and mass-produced food defined the zone over a steel works.
1960s.note: Reclaimed tidal flats drew steel, oil storage and food plants.

today.name: Funabashi and Ichikawa shore
lines: Food plants and truck logistics.
today.note: Food plants and warehouses dominate; the Keiyō food complex holds 29 firms.

1960s.name: Kimitsu steelworks
lines: An integrated steelworks.
1960s.note: Yawata Steel's Kimitsu works opened in 1965 on new landfill.

today.name: Kimitsu steelworks
lines: Blast furnaces still make steel.
today.note: Nippon Steel's Kimitsu works still runs blast furnaces.
